strengths: Well-motivated problem: Compelling visual evidence (Figure 1) demonstrating that existing LSNM methods fail under skewed noise, showing residual dependence in the true causal direction

Methodologically sound approach: Natural extension of LSNMs from Gaussian to skew-normal noise with backward compatibility; proper use of B-splines and principled ECM adaptation for parameter estimation

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Novel synthetic datasets with three skewness levels, 11 baselines, ablation studies showing ECM necessity (28-34% improvements on LSs-IT), and both synthetic and established benchmarks
Exceptional performance on skewed noise: SKEWD-LL achieves 100% accuracy across all synthetic skewed-noise datasets while competitors degrade significantly (ROCHE: 81%, QCCD: 11% on LSs(1.750))
Strong reproducibility and presentation: Publicly available code promised, detailed hyperparameter specifications, thorough appendices, informative visualizations
weaknesses: Severely restricted scope: Limited to bivariate causal discovery, which is a significant limitation for a top venue; multivariate extension essential for real-world applicability

Computational complexity not addressed: Multi-stage optimization (Bayesian optimization → CMA-ES → ECM) lacks runtime comparisons with baselines; no scalability analysis provided; practical feasibility unclear

Incremental methodological novelty: Primary components (skew-normal distribution, B-splines, ECM) are well-established; main contribution is combining existing techniques for LSNMs, which feels somewhat incremental

Bounded skewness limitation: Skew-normal restricted to |γ₁| ≈ 0.9953, while many real distributions (e.g., exponential with γ₁=2) exceed this bound; limited applicability to heavily skewed real-world data

Modest improvements on real benchmarks: ROCHE outperforms SKEWD-LL on established benchmarks (87.69% vs 77.43%); SKEWD-IT achieves only 2.67% improvement, raising questions about practical significance

Experimental design concerns: Synthetic data generation follows existing baselines' schemes (potential bias); IGCI-G's perfect accuracy despite being 'highly misspecified' suggests dataset bias; limited real-world validation (only 99 Tübingen pairs)

Insufficient justification of assumptions: Likelihood scoring assumes Gaussian marginals without empirical verification; B-spline knot counts (q=14, p=7) appear arbitrary; bounds on λ and ρ lack principled justification
Missing statistical rigor: No significance tests between methods despite overlapping confidence intervals; no analysis of distributional assumptions' validity in practice
Limited real-world applicability: No experiments on domains with known skewed noise (e.g., economic, environmental data); identifiability assertions not explicitly verified for skew-normal case

strengths: Identifies and clearly demonstrates a practical problem overlooked in existing literature—that standard LSNM methods assume symmetric noise distributions, which is violated in real-world domains
Comprehensive experimental validation including novel synthetic benchmarks with controlled skewness levels, 13 established benchmarks, multiple SOTA baselines, and thorough ablation studies
Two complementary inference variants (likelihood-based and independence-based) providing flexibility for different settings
Technically sound adaptation of ECM algorithms for GAM parameter estimation in the skew-normal setting
Honest discussion of method limitations including marginal Gaussianity assumptions, scalability constraints, and potential model misspecification
Novel contribution of benchmark datasets with varying skewness levels (γ₁ ∈ {-0.455, 0.985, 1.750}) useful for future research
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—primarily applies existing techniques (skew-normal distributions, ECM algorithms, GAMs) to an existing model class rather than developing fundamentally new methods

Concerning empirical results: method underperforms SOTA on established benchmarks (Table 1, 85.02% vs. ROCHE's 87.69%), suggesting overspecialization to skewed noise problem with unclear practical benefit on realistic data

Complex three-step optimization (Bayesian optimization → CMA-ES → ECM) lacks full justification; unclear why simpler alternatives (e.g., direct ECM with cross-validation) are insufficient; no computational cost comparisons

Strong marginal Gaussianity assumption in likelihood scoring relies on asymptotic results; violations on finite samples acknowledged in appendix but not addressed; ablation shows KDE marginals significantly improve performance on non-Gaussian data

Multivariate extension (SKEWD-MV) is limited and ad-hoc: depends entirely on PC algorithm for MEC estimation, only evaluated on synthetic data (d≤10), acknowledged to have exponential scalability limitations, lacks real-world multivariate validation

Model misspecification concerns: skew-normal bounded to γ₁ ≈ 0.9953 but tests on GNO distributions with γ₁=1.750; GNO also exhibits different tail behavior and excess kurtosis; paper demonstrates robustness but doesn't characterize when such misspecification is acceptable
Identifiability analysis entirely relies on existing work without characterizing when skew-normal LSNMs specifically help or hurt identifiability beyond general LSNM results
Lack of real-world validation: no application to actual datasets with known skewed noise properties despite citing examples; only real data evaluation is on Tübingen bivariate pairs

IGCI-G anomaly unexplained: achieves comparable performance to SKEWD on skewed datasets (100%) despite being described as 'highly misspecified,' suggesting either incomplete analysis or baseline implementation issues
